teaser.text: Waste Management sells a dependable way to move, treat, contain and sometimes recover unwanted material. A dollar enters through collection and specialized service fees, through sales of recovered products and energy, and leaves through the labor, fuel, facilities and outside disposal that make those services possible.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for WM?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA is the main operating driver. The base case rises from $8,550 million in October 2027 to $9,250 million in October 2029. That is slower than WM’s recent growth record, because price and productivity must offset subdued volume while healthcare integration and sustainability projects develop gradually. Adjusted EBITDA rose every year from 2021 through 2025, and 2026 guidance is $8.15–$8.25 billion. The bear case gives $8,000 million, $7,850 million and $8,000 million as volume, retention and healthcare risks weigh. The bull case gives $8,800 million, $9,500 million and $10,250 million if projects connect and ramp on schedule.

paragraphs.text: An analyst can also subtract stock compensation as an allowance for ownership given to employees. This produces a stricter measure of cash available to shareholders, even though the deduction is not another cash payment. Across the five-year period, that stricter cash measure grew, but it declined as a share of revenue.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for WM today?

paragraphs.text: At $224.19 on October 16, 2026, WM is priced as a dependable business, not as an obvious bargain.

The trailing P/E compares the share price with earnings already reported. The forward P/E looks cheaper because it uses expected earnings, which may reflect real improvement, lower integration costs, less interest expense, or optimistic forecasts. Stericycle complicates the comparison: acquired customer relationships are amortized over time, while integration costs can involve real cash spending.

blocks.heading: How much does WM pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise from $4.20 per share in October 2027 to $5.08 in October 2029 in the base case. The bear case freezes the current $3.78 annual rate; the bull case reaches $5.43. WM has raised its dividend for twenty-three consecutive years, but capital needs and debt argue for slower growth than the 2026 increase.

blocks.heading: Is WM's dividend covered by its cash flow?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and paying for capital expenditure. Across the period, WM generated $11.182 billion of it, while dividends and buybacks consumed $10.141 billion. That left less internally generated cash for acquisitions and debt reduction.

Free cash flow is the money left after operating the business and investing in it, although WM also includes proceeds from selling assets. In the second quarter, WM reported $1.10 billion of free cash flow and returned $1.04 billion to shareholders. The dividend is therefore not an extra cash pile; dividends, buybacks and debt repayment compete for the same dollars.

The 31.8x trailing P/E rests against a 24.8x forward P/E that requires expected earnings improvement. The turn is that diluted EPS fell in 2025 while the company’s own real free cash flow per share rose; debt also rose sharply with Stericycle while cash remained small.

earnings.title: WM earnings: guidance and what to watch
earnings.meta_description: WM expects October 27, 2026 results to test revenue, ordinary collection volumes and its 2026 guidance.
earnings.opening: WM's next results are expected on October 27, 2026. Watch whether ordinary collection volumes improve while WM holds its profitability guidance.
earnings.closing: The full WM memo also covers its business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: For 2026, management guides to $26.275–$26.475 billion of revenue, $8.15–$8.25 billion of adjusted operating EBITDA and $3.75–$3.85 billion of free cash flow. That outlook assumes 5.4%–5.8% core price but only 3.2%–3.6% yield, putting customer retention and ordinary volume at the center of execution.

On July 28, WM lowered full-year revenue guidance to **$26.275–$26.475 billion** while keeping its adjusted operating EBITDA target at **$8.15–$8.25 billion**. Adjusted operating EBITDA is operating earnings before interest, taxes and selected accounting charges; free cash flow is cash left after operating cash flow, capital spending and asset-sale proceeds. Holding those targets with fewer sales dollars implies an adjusted margin of **31.0%–31.2%**.

blocks.heading: Has WM kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: WM then promised to resume buybacks and bring leverage back to its target range. Leverage of 2.96 times means debt was about 2.96 times annual operating EBITDA, a measure of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization. By midyear, WM had repurchased US$1 billion and reported leverage within its 2.5–3.0 target range. That is tangible progress, though the full-year promise still depends on cash generation and service performance.

blocks.heading: What do WM's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: That pattern has persisted. Revenue missed in four consecutive quarters from the third quarter of 2025 through the second quarter of 2026, while earnings missed twice and then beat twice. Higher prices, lower costs, automation or repurchases can protect profit while the sales trend weakens. A shop can produce more profit per remaining share without selling more goods.

blocks.heading: What should you watch in WM's next results?

paragraphs.text: The immediate checkpoint is the **October 27, 2026** earnings release and the following day’s call. Investors should look for revenue meeting expectations, ordinary collection volumes improving and gas plants moving into commercial operation. Fourth-quarter results should also clarify whether 2027 earnings come from completed facilities or from further construction and favourable commodity prices.
